newsitem.title: USA: Minn. lawmakers reach education funding accord.
newsitem.headline: Minn. lawmakers reach education funding accord.

text.p: Minnesota Gov. Arne Carlson and legislative leaders have reached an agreement to end a dispute over a portion of the $6.7 billion biennium budget for elementary and secondary education.
Carlson and the leaders announced the agreement Wednesday night on the eve of a special session to resolve the dispute.
Lawmakers are scheduled to open the session at 1130 EDT and hope to adjourn with a final agreement by 1300 EDT Friday.
Carlson had vetoed the entire education funding package earlier in June because it lacked $150 million of tax credits he had proposed that included private school tuitions.

The agreement announced by Carlson, House Speaker Phil Carruthers, Senate Majority Leader Roger Moe and House Minority Leader Steve Sviggum adds $75 million of credits provided that revenue forecasts show that funding is available.
"This agreement is a big step forward in giving all Minnesota parents more educational choices," Carlson said in a statement.

The agreement calls for allowing education tax deductions for computer software and hardware, tutoring and education summer camps. It also increases current deductions to $1,625 for elementary pupils and $2,500 for secondary students beginning in the 1998 tax year.
The agreement also calls for expanding working family credits and introduces a refundable education tax credit for families with incomes of $33,500 or less beginning in the 1998 tax year.
The new refundable credit would provide $1,000 per child and up to $2,000 per family and applies to all items under the tax deduction except tuition for private schools.

Carlson had proposed tripling current deductions and all credits to be used for hiring a tutor, summer school programs, purchase of a home computer for educational needs or tuition to private schools.

Moody's Investors Service reported Tuesday that the dispute would have no effect on the financial stability of Minnesota's school districts even if it remained unresolved before the start of the new fiscal biennium Tuesday.

The school districts would still have received 93 percent of their previous year's funding and Minnesota law would have guaranteed payments of debt service on bonds issued by the districts from the state's general fund, Moody's noted.
